newsitem.title: BELGIUM: Debate sharpens over post-EMU monetary order.
newsitem.headline: Debate sharpens over post-EMU monetary order.

text.p: Questions and doubts remain about the prospects for the successful launch of Europe's planned single currency, but the way the euro might alter global monetary relations is coming into sharper focus.
Many of the ideas being offered are inevitably speculative and are likely to be modified well before the expected launch of economic and monetary union (EMU) in January 1999.
Views have begun to emerge on how the euro might be managed against the dollar and the yen, the two leading currencies outside the 15-nation European Union.

Speaking to Royal Institute of International Affairs in London, Belgian Finance Minister Philippe Maystadt last week suggested that the major industrialised powers may have to consider more explicit targeting of their currencies.

"I am...convinced that it might become useful, at some time, to declare what could be considered as 'target zones' or, in more cautious terms, 'plausibility zones' for the exchange rate of the major currencies," Maystadt said.

Maystadt, who is also chairman of the International Monetary Fund's interim committee, said the Fund could play a central role in monitoring excessive exchange rate movements and potentially coordinate any policy response from the United States, Japan and countries inside EMU.

Echoing the need to perhaps reconsider the free-floating exchange rate regime among the Group of Seven industrialised countries are several American economists, some of whom believe EMU will pose a number of policy challenges for the United States.
In a recent study for the Washington-based Institute for International Economics, economist C. Randall Henning argued that EMU could lead to undesirable turbulence between the dollar and the euro.

To counter potential misalignments, Henning said both the EU and the United States should eventually specify "a range of exchange rates beyond which fluctuations would be regarded as clearly not justified by the fundamentals."

Analysts note that the idea of informal or even explicit currency targets is one that G7 countries -- the United States, Japan, Germany, France, Britain, Italy and Canada -- have considered in the past, but never with any meaningful results.

One of dangers of specifying trading limits, say some experts, is that it provides currency markets with a target they can easily challenge. Such clarity of policy intentions could in turn lead to greater market turbulence and become self-defeating.

Combined with uncertainty about what the proper value for the euro will be against the dollar or the yen, this makes it doubtful that European monetary authorities will agree to a more managed monetary system.

"Current thinking in continental circles about what the exchange rate policy of the (European Central Bank) might be certainly excludes any sort of pegging to the dollar or the yen," said Juergen von Hagen, economist at Bonn's Centre for European Integration Studies.

Von Hagen added that it was hard to imagine a scenario where American policy-makers would sign up to closer exchange rate cooperation without a clear understanding by European officials about the equilibrium value for the euro against non-EMU nations.

The difficulty will be calculating the value of the euro against other major currencies that reflects the economic fundamentals of EMU nations against those of countries like Japan and the United States.

Compounding the difficulties in determining an appropriate level for the euro is the current debate in Europe over the future European Central Bank (ECB) and the emphasis it should give to price stability, its stated mandate.

The new French government, led by Prime Minister Lionel Jospin, has argued forcefully for a political counterweight to the ECB in order to steer economic policy among euro members in the proper direction.

Yet France's emphasis on jobs and growth conflicts with the hard money concerns of officials in Frankfurt and Bonn, who believe that any move towards politicising the euro would undercut its value and weaken much-needed public confidence.

Some note the ECB might find itself in the dark when guiding monetary policy in the early stages of EMU. It will be operating with economic and monetary data aggregated from up to eight to 10 countries that might prove unreliable at first and require several years of refinement.
